targets.title: Any authenticated caller (GET /api/lab/secure/whoami)
targets.description: Needs authentication only. Reports what Spring Security made of the token: the authorities built from the database next to the role claim the token carried.

targets.title: Teacher area (GET /api/lab/secure/teacher-area)
targets.description: Authenticated callers whose stored role is TEACHER or ADMIN.

targets.title: Admin area (GET /api/lab/secure/admin-area)
targets.description: Authenticated callers whose stored role is ADMIN.

variants.title: Valid token
variants.description: Signed with the lab key, correct issuer, expires in five minutes.

variants.title: Expired token
variants.description: Correctly signed, but exp is ten minutes in the past (beyond the decoder's 60 second clock skew).

variants.title: Token not valid yet
variants.description: Correctly signed, but nbf (not before) is ten minutes in the future.

variants.title: Signed with a different key
variants.description: Well-formed and unexpired, but signed with a key the lab decoder does not know.

variants.title: Wrong issuer
variants.description: Correctly signed, but the iss claim names a different issuer.

variants.title: Tampered signature
variants.description: A valid token with one character of the signature changed.

variants.title: Tampered payload (forged role claim)
variants.description: The payload is replaced with one claiming a different role while the original signature is kept.

variants.title: Malformed token
variants.description: Only two dot-separated parts: the signature is missing, so it is not a compact JWT.

variants.title: Unsigned token (alg none)
variants.description: The header declares alg none and there is no signature, hoping the server skips verification.

variants.title: No token
variants.description: The request carries no Authorization header at all.

experiments.title: A valid token
experiments.changes: A correctly signed lab token for your own username is sent to a lab endpoint.
experiments.consequence: The decoder accepts the token, the application's converter reads your current role and enabled flag from the database (one SQL statement), the authorities are stored in the SecurityContext, the rule allows an authenticated caller and the controller runs. This is the baseline every other experiment is compared with.

experiments.title: An expired token
experiments.changes: The token's exp claim lies ten minutes in the past. The signature is still correct.
experiments.consequence: The decoder verifies the signature first and then its timestamp validator rejects the expired token, so Spring Security answers 401 and the challenge says the Jwt expired. The converter never runs, so no SQL is prepared and no controller is entered. A valid signature does not make an old token acceptable.

experiments.title: A token that is not valid yet
experiments.changes: The token's nbf (not before) claim lies ten minutes in the future.
experiments.consequence: The same timestamp validator that checks exp also checks nbf, so a token used before its start time is refused with 401 before the converter or any controller runs and without any SQL.

experiments.title: A token signed with the wrong key
experiments.changes: The token is well formed and unexpired but was signed with a different secret than the decoder uses.
experiments.consequence: HS256 is a keyed hash: only a holder of the verifying secret can produce a signature it accepts. Verification fails, the answer is 401 and nothing after the decoder runs (no SQL, no controller). This is what protects SpringLab if someone invents a token without knowing its secret.

experiments.title: A token from the wrong issuer
experiments.changes: The signature is correct, but the iss claim names a different issuer.
experiments.consequence: Signature verification passes, then the issuer validator rejects the token because iss is not the expected value. A correct signature proves who signed the token, not that it was meant for this application. The result is a 401 with no SQL and no controller.

experiments.title: A tampered signature
experiments.changes: One character inside the signature of a valid token is changed.
experiments.consequence: The recomputed signature no longer matches the one in the token, so the decoder rejects it and Spring Security answers 401 without a database lookup or a controller.

experiments.title: A forged role claim in the payload
experiments.changes: The payload is replaced so the role claim says a different role (ADMIN when yours is lower), keeping the original signature.
experiments.consequence: The payload is only Base64URL-encoded, so anyone can read and rewrite it; what they cannot do is make the signature match the new content. Verification fails and the answer is 401. The forgery is stopped by the signature, before any role is even considered.

experiments.title: A malformed token
experiments.changes: The token has only two dot-separated parts, so it is not a compact JWT.
experiments.consequence: The decoder cannot even parse it. The answer is 401, the challenge reports a decoding problem, and nothing else runs.

experiments.title: An unsigned token (alg none)
experiments.changes: The header declares alg none and the token has no signature, hoping verification is skipped.
experiments.consequence: The decoder is configured for HS256 only. It refuses an unsecured JWT instead of trusting the algorithm named in the token, so the answer is 401 with no SQL and no controller. The algorithm must be decided by the server, never by the token.

experiments.title: No token at all
experiments.changes: The request is sent without an Authorization header.
experiments.consequence: BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter has nothing to authenticate, so the request continues as anonymous. The rule requires an authenticated caller, so it is refused with 401. The challenge is a bare 'Bearer' with no token error, because no token was presented. No SQL is prepared.

experiments.title: A student attempts an admin-only endpoint
experiments.changes: A valid token whose role claim is honest (it matches your stored role) is sent to the admin-only lab endpoint. The outcome depends on your role.
experiments.consequence: Authentication succeeds: the token is valid and your role is read from the database (one SQL statement). Authorization then compares that role with the rule for the path. Students and teachers get 403 Forbidden and the controller does not run; an administrator gets 200. 401 means 'who are you?'; 403 means 'I know who you are, and the answer is no'.

experiments.title: A validly signed token that claims ADMIN
experiments.changes: A correctly signed token whose role claim says ADMIN is sent to the admin-only endpoint, whatever your real role is.
experiments.consequence: The signature is valid, so the token is authentic, but its role claim is only information. SpringLab builds the authorities from the role stored in the database, so a non-admin is still refused with 403 even though the token says ADMIN. The claim is not authoritative: the database is.

experiments.title: A token that claims less than the database says
experiments.changes: A correctly signed token whose role claim says STUDENT is sent to the admin-only endpoint.
experiments.consequence: The database wins in both directions. If you are an administrator you are still admitted (200) although the token says STUDENT; if you are not, you are refused (403). Roles come from the users table on every request, never from the token.

experiments.title: Role-based access to the teacher area
experiments.changes: A valid token is sent to the endpoint that needs the TEACHER or ADMIN role.
experiments.consequence: Students receive 403; teachers and administrators receive 200. The rule is hasAnyRole('TEACHER', 'ADMIN') and is evaluated against the authorities built from the database.

experiments.title: What if the signing secret leaked?
experiments.changes: An attacker learns the HS256 secret that the application uses to sign and verify tokens.
experiments.consequence: Anyone holding the secret can mint a validly signed token for any subject. Because SpringLab takes authorities from the database, a forged role claim would not raise anyone's privileges, but a token whose subject is an administrator's username would authenticate as that administrator until the secret is rotated. That is why the secret must be long and random, supplied through an environment variable, never logged and never sent to a browser. This experiment is SIMULATED on purpose: the application's real signing key is never used for lab tokens.
experiments.realBehaviourReference: RFC 7518 section 3.2 (HMAC with SHA-2: key requirements) and RFC 7519 (JSON Web Token).

experiments.title: What if tokens used RS256 instead of HS256?
experiments.changes: Tokens would be signed with an RSA private key and verified with the matching public key.
experiments.consequence: Verifiers could validate tokens without being able to create them, which suits several services or a separate authorization server; the cost is key management. SpringLab is one application that both issues and verifies tokens, so a shared secret is sufficient. Switching would mean giving the decoder a public key or JWK Set and the encoder a private key. This experiment is SIMULATED: it describes a configuration this application does not contain.
experiments.realBehaviourReference: Spring Security reference, OAuth 2.0 Resource Server (JWT): specifying the verification key or JWK Set URI; RFC 7518 section 3.3 (RS256).

experiments.title: What if an account is disabled while its token is still valid?
experiments.changes: An administrator disables an account whose access token has not expired.
experiments.consequence: A purely stateless JWT stays valid until exp, because nothing is looked up. SpringLab's converter checks the enabled flag in the database on every authenticated request, so the very next request is answered with 401. SpringLab's own integration tests demonstrate this (disablingAccountRejectsExistingTokenImmediately); the simulator does not, because disabling real accounts from a lesson would not be safe.
experiments.realBehaviourReference: SpringLab test JwtAuthenticationIntegrationTest.disablingAccountRejectsExistingTokenImmediately; Phase 3 design notes in the README.
